main.title: Metroid Prime 2: Echoes
main.summary: Metroid Prime 2: Echoes is a 2004 action-adventure game developed by Retro Studios and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.

cards.heading: Metroid Prime 2: Echoes
cards.text: Metroid Prime 2: Echoes is a 2004 action-adventure game developed by Retro Studios and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. It is the sixth main Metroid game, and was released in North America, Europe and Australia in late 2004. In Japan, it was released in May 2005 as Metroid Prime 2: Dark Echoes.

cards.heading: Aether and its hostile other dimension
cards.text: The story follows the bounty hunter Samus Aran after she is sent to rescue Galactic Federation Marines from a ship near Aether, a planet inhabited by a race known as the Luminoth. She discovers that the troops were slaughtered by the Ing, a hostile race that came from an alternate dimension of Aether. Samus must travel to four temples to ensure the destruction of the evil Ing, while battling them, wild creatures, Space Pirates, and her mysterious doppelgänger, Dark Samus.

cards.heading: Atmosphere, difficulty and multiplayer
cards.text: Retro sought to differentiate Echoes with a heavier focus on storytelling, new gameplay mechanics, and a multiplayer feature. Nintendo launched a viral marketing campaign that included several websites written as if taking place in the Metroid universe. The single-player mode was acclaimed for its graphics, atmosphere and music, though its steep difficulty and multiplayer mode were criticized.

cards.heading: Reception and legacy
cards.text: Echoes received several awards and spots on "top games" lists by Nintendo Power and IGN. More than 1.10 million copies were sold worldwide. A sequel, Metroid Prime 3: Corruption was released in 2007. In 2009, an enhanced version of Echoes was released for Wii in Japan and as part of Metroid Prime: Trilogy.

main.title: Fantasy Westward Journey
main.summary: Fantasy Westward Journey is a massively multiplayer online role-playing game (MMORPG) developed and operated by the Chinese company NetEase.

cards.text: Fantasy Westward Journey is a massively multiplayer online role-playing game (MMORPG) developed and operated by the Chinese company NetEase. The Windows game entered public open beta on 18 December 2003, followed by commercial operation in January 2004. The game is the most popular online game in China as of May 2007 by peak concurrent users (PCU), with a peak count of 1.5 million. Registered users reached 25 million by April 2005, with 576,000 peak concurrent players on 198 game servers, which was considered the fastest-growing online game in China at the time. Average concurrent users were reported in August 2006 to be around 400,000.

The game uses the same engine as Westward Journey II, albeit with a distinctively different graphical style. Both games are inspired by the 16th-century Chinese novel Journey to the West. Together with Westward Journey II, it is one of the highest-grossing video games of all time, having earned an estimated $6.5 billion in lifetime revenue as of 2019 and having 400 million users as of 2015.

main.title: Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney – Trials and Tribulations
main.summary: Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney – Trials and Tribulations is a visual novel adventure video game developed and published by Capcom.

cards.text: Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney – Trials and Tribulations is a visual novel adventure video game developed and published by Capcom. It was originally released for the Game Boy Advance in 2004 in Japan, and has since been released for several platforms, including a Nintendo DS version that was released in 2007 in Japan and North America and in 2008 in Europe. It is the third game in the Ace Attorney series, following Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney (2001) and Justice for All (2002).

The story follows defense attorneys Phoenix Wright and Mia Fey, who defend their clients in five episodes. Among other characters are Phoenix's assistant and Mia's sister Maya, her cousin Pearl, and prosecutor Godot. The gameplay is split into courtroom sections, where the player cross-examines witnesses and tries to discover contradictions in their testimonies, and investigations, where they gather evidence and talk to witnesses.

The game was directed and written by Shu Takumi as the last game in an Ace Attorney trilogy; he also wanted it to be the final entry in the series, as he felt he had explored Phoenix's character fully. Because he was satisfied with the gameplay in Justice for All, he did not introduce any new gameplay mechanics in Trials and Tribulations. Flashbacks were used as a major theme in the game; this originated in Takumi trying to come up with a way of handling dialogue-integrated tutorials, and deciding to use a flashback to a case from when Mia was a rookie attorney.

The game has received generally favorable reviews, with reviewers liking the story, writing, character designs and music, but with some criticizing the lack of new gameplay mechanics. Additionally, the Wii version was criticized for using resized graphics from the Nintendo DS version, without any modifications to make them appear better on a larger screen. The Nintendo DS version was a commercial success in North America, with pre-orders being more than double the amount Capcom had estimated.

A high-definition version of the first three Ace Attorney games, Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney Trilogy HD, was released for iOS and Android in Japan on February 7, 2012, and for iOS in the West on May 30, 2013. Another collection of the first three games, Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney Trilogy, was released for the Nintendo 3DS in Japan on April 17, 2014, in North America on December 9, 2014, and in Europe on December 11, 2014. It was also released for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, and Xbox One on February 21, 2019, in Japan, and on April 9, 2019, internationally; a Windows version was released internationally on the same date. The PC version of the collection was among the best-selling new releases of the month on Steam.

main.title: Breakdown
main.summary: Derrick Cole escapes a research facility through first-person exploration, physical interactions and close combat.

cards.heading: Breakdown
cards.text: Breakdown is Namco's first-person action adventure for the original Xbox, released in 2004. Derrick Cole wakes in a research facility with no memory of how he arrived. His escape develops through shooting, close combat and increasingly unusual physical abilities, with the camera following his actions from inside his own body.

cards.heading: Hands in front of the camera
cards.text: Picking up supplies takes more than walking over them. Derrick reaches down for objects, brings food or drink into view and uses it before the action resumes. The same perspective follows him onto ladders and through doors. These small movements give the laboratory a physical scale: a can on a table is something his hand must reach, while an approaching enemy makes the time spent collecting it feel much longer.

cards.heading: A fight at arm's length
cards.text: With his fists raised, Derrick fights close enough for an enemy to fill the screen. Target locking keeps that opponent in view while the triggers and movement inputs produce punches, kicks and combinations. Guarding or evading creates the opening for another attack, but another enemy outside the narrow view can interrupt it. The most useful position is therefore part of the fight itself: keep the immediate opponent within reach without letting the others arrive from behind.

cards.heading: Looking for a way out
cards.text: Alex accompanies Derrick through a facility whose corridors, shafts and ruined spaces demand different kinds of movement. Watching her reach another ledge can reveal the direction of travel, while Derrick still needs to find his own way across. At other moments, the camera follows a fall or a struggle closely enough to interrupt that sense of control. The route out becomes tied to understanding what his body can do, as the research behind his abilities draws the escape into a larger mystery.

main.title: Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen
main.subtitle: The first region returns with new routes beyond its familiar towns
main.summary: Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen rebuild the original Kanto adventure for Game Boy Advance. Released in Japan on 29 January 2004, Game Freak's paired games begin with Professor Oak, a first partner and a rival setting out from Pallet Town. Colourful new graphics accompany a familiar route through Gyms and Team Rocket's schemes, with the Sevii Islands extending the journey.

cards.heading: Back to Kanto
cards.text: Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen rebuild the original Kanto adventure for Game Boy Advance. Released in Japan on 29 January 2004, Game Freak's paired games begin with Professor Oak, a first partner and a rival setting out from Pallet Town. Colourful new graphics accompany a familiar route through Gyms and Team Rocket's schemes, with the Sevii Islands extending the journey.

cards.heading: A party takes shape
cards.text: Choosing Bulbasaur, Charmander or Squirtle gives the first few battles a different balance. The party then grows through encounters in grass, caves and water, with each capture adding another possible answer to a Gym Leader. Returning players recognise the geography and many of its obstacles. Changes in presentation and the expanded range of information make the same towns easier to read as places within a connected journey.

cards.heading: The islands beyond
cards.text: The Sevii Islands add destinations beyond Kanto's established mainland. Travelling between them brings further encounters and places to investigate, opening the remake outward as its adventure progresses. Their presence gives an experienced player something to discover alongside the pleasure of remembering a route. The return to an older region becomes part of the Game Boy Advance generation, with connections to the other contemporary games expanding which partners can join a collection.

cards.heading: Trading without a cable
cards.text: The Wireless Adapter lets nearby players trade and battle without a physical Game Link Cable. Meeting in the Union Room makes that exchange visible as a shared place inside the game. FireRed and LeafGreen keep different encounter lists, encouraging players to compare their catches. A creature raised on one cartridge can become a friend's missing entry or a new member of another party, giving the paired releases a practical relationship.

main.title: Metroid: Zero Mission
main.summary: Samus returns to Zebes in a reconstruction of the first Metroid, with new routes, more agile movement and a story that continues beyond Mother Brain.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: Metroid: Zero Mission is Nintendo R&D1's 2004 action-adventure for Game Boy Advance. It retells the first Metroid, returning bounty hunter Samus Aran to the planet Zebes with a rebuilt world, a wider range of abilities and an additional chapter beyond the original ending.

cards.heading: Back to Zebes
cards.text: Samus Aran lands alone on Zebes to stop the Space Pirates from turning the Metroids into weapons. Zero Mission revisits the mission introduced in the 1986 Metroid, rebuilding its underground world for Game Boy Advance. Brinstar's caverns lead towards the heat of Norfair and the fortress of Tourian, with elevators connecting places that gradually become familiar. A door passed on the way in may become the reason to return later: progress comes from learning the shape of the planet as well as defeating its inhabitants.

cards.heading: A new ability changes the route
cards.text: The Morph Ball lets Samus roll into tunnels beneath the main passages; bombs reveal openings in apparently solid floors. Missiles, the Power Grip and further upgrades keep changing which routes she can reach. Ledge grabbing makes a narrow opening above her head a usable entrance, while diagonal aiming lets her deal with enemies without standing directly in front of them. The map records explored rooms and Chozo statues point towards destinations, leaving the player to work out how the passages connect and where an upgrade might help.

cards.heading: Beyond the original escape
cards.text: Zero Mission also gives this early adventure a visual story of its own. Illustrated scenes draw attention to Samus and the Space Pirates between stretches of exploration, while the familiar locations and creatures return with new sprites and backgrounds. Defeating Mother Brain opens an additional part of the adventure: Samus loses her armour and must evade the pirates with a much more limited weapon. The change gives the suit's familiar strength a different meaning when it is regained, extending the first game's escape into a new final act.

main.title: Champions of Norrath
main.subtitle: Enter Norrath with a smaller party
main.summary: Champions of Norrath is Snowblind Studios' PlayStation 2 action role-playing game, first released in North America on 10 February 2004. Set in the EverQuest universe, it gives a single player or a cooperative group a direct journey through forests, settlements and dungeons. Choosing a character begins a cycle of fighting, gathering equipment and improving abilities. The world supplies a larger fantasy setting without requiring the player to join the online role-playing game from which it came. Its adventure is organised around a small party moving together towards the next encounter.

cards.heading: Enter Norrath with a smaller party
cards.text: Champions of Norrath is Snowblind Studios' PlayStation 2 action role-playing game, first released in North America on 10 February 2004. Set in the EverQuest universe, it gives a single player or a cooperative group a direct journey through forests, settlements and dungeons. Choosing a character begins a cycle of fighting, gathering equipment and improving abilities. The world supplies a larger fantasy setting without requiring the player to join the online role-playing game from which it came. Its adventure is organised around a small party moving together towards the next encounter.

cards.heading: Find equipment that changes the next fight
cards.text: A character's race, appearance and abilities establish the starting point, while experience and discovered equipment guide later development. Monsters leave rewards that make the next stretch of the journey more manageable, connecting exploration to practical improvement. Different party members can contribute different strengths during cooperative play. The player therefore considers both the next useful item and how the group works when several threats arrive together. A familiar dungeon becomes a place to search carefully because the contents can change what a character is capable of doing afterwards.

cards.heading: A shared adventure from Snowblind
cards.text: The game expands the technology used for Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance, carrying Snowblind's console action-role-playing approach into Norrath. Up to four players can cooperate, with the PlayStation 2 Network Adapter originally enabling online groups as well as local play. Inon Zur composed the music. Ubisoft published the European edition in June 2004, and Champions: Return to Arms followed in 2005. The original's appeal is straightforward and durable: a party enters a dangerous place together, emerges with better equipment and immediately has another reason to see what lies beyond it.

main.title: Shadow Hearts: Covenant
main.subtitle: A curse during the Great War
main.summary: Shadow Hearts: Covenant is Nautilus's PlayStation 2 role-playing game, first released in Japan on 19 February 2004. Set in 1915, it continues Yuri Hyuga's story as the First World War reaches the village he protects. German lieutenant Karin Koenig becomes involved in his struggle against a secret society, and a curse threatens the powers that once defined him. The adventure travels through an alternate Europe and Asia, combining historical surroundings with monsters, eccentric allies and supernatural plots. Its darker events share space with conspicuously comic episodes.

cards.heading: A curse during the Great War
cards.text: Shadow Hearts: Covenant is Nautilus's PlayStation 2 role-playing game, first released in Japan on 19 February 2004. Set in 1915, it continues Yuri Hyuga's story as the First World War reaches the village he protects. German lieutenant Karin Koenig becomes involved in his struggle against a secret society, and a curse threatens the powers that once defined him. The adventure travels through an alternate Europe and Asia, combining historical surroundings with monsters, eccentric allies and supernatural plots. Its darker events share space with conspicuously comic episodes.

cards.heading: A party working around the ring
cards.text: Four characters can take part in a turn-based battle. Their actions again depend on the Judgement Ring: the player times button presses as an indicator crosses the marked areas. Covenant expands the system with character combinations, allowing party members to link attacks into a longer sequence. Position and the order of actions become more important when building those chains. The timing mechanic keeps the player involved during an attack, while the party's different abilities provide the decisions that come before the button presses.

cards.heading: Give each companion a different role
cards.text: Yuri can still transform, while other companions bring their own unusual skills and personal side activities. Those differences make the travelling party a collection of people with distinct habits rather than interchangeable attackers. Returning director and writer Matsuzo Machida adjusted both tone and mechanics in response to the first game's reception. Miyako Kato returned as character artist, with music led by Yoshitaka Hirota alongside Yasunori Mitsuda and Kenji Ito. Critics particularly valued its characters and battle system, and the series continued with From the New World in 2005.

main.title: Onimusha 3: Demon Siege
main.summary: Onimusha 3: Demon Siege, released in Japan and Europe as Onimusha 3, is a 2004 action-adventure game developed and published by Capcom.

cards.heading: Onimusha 3: Demon Siege
cards.text: Onimusha 3: Demon Siege, released in Japan and Europe as Onimusha 3, is a 2004 action-adventure game developed and published by Capcom. It is the third game of the Onimusha series and was released for the PlayStation 2 in April 2004, and later ported to Windows in December 2005. The story focuses on the returning hero, swordsman Hidemitsu Samanosuke Akechi, who is on a quest to defeat Nobunaga Oda, who wishes to conquer Japan with his army of demons known as Genma. Samanosuke, however, changes places with a French officer from the future named Jacques Blanc, and both have to adapt to their new worlds to defeat the Genma army and stop Oda Nobunaga's ambitions to conquer the world.

cards.heading: Two heroes exchange items across time
cards.text: The game retains elements from previous games in the franchise including the use of multiple special weapons in order to fight enemies and absorb their energy to enhance the weaponry. This time the player primarily controls both Samanosuke and Jacques in separate scenarios. The two are able to exchange items in order to solve puzzles. In order to appeal to the Western market, the team set this game in Paris and chose French actor Jean Reno to portray Jacques.

cards.heading: Three-dimensional combat and a choreographed opening
cards.text: Onimusha 3 has been generally well received by video game publications. Most of the writers' praise focused on the improved controls and the use of a 3D engine that allowed better combat and visuals. Critics also highly praised the CGI intro cutscene, which had martial arts legend Donnie Yen directing the fight sequences.

cards.heading: Reception and legacy
cards.text: One of the main criticisms was the game's very short length. The game also generated good sales, with over 1.5 million copies sold as of May 2008, although according to Capcom it did not sell as much as they had hoped for.

main.title: MTX Mototrax
main.summary: MTX Mototrax is a racing video game developed by Left Field Productions and published by Activision for PlayStation 2 and Xbox in 2004.

cards.text: MTX Mototrax is a racing video game developed by Left Field Productions and published by Activision for PlayStation 2 and Xbox in 2004. It was released for Microsoft Windows and Mac OS X later that year developed by Beenox and published by Aspyr. It was also released in 2006 for the PlayStation Portable. Additional releases were planned for the GameCube console in 2004, which was later canceled, and Tapwave Zodiac, which was called off when Tapwave went out of business. A demo version of the game is available in the options menu in the PlayStation 2 version of Tony Hawk's Underground.

The game was developed in partnership with motocross rider Travis Pastrana, who lent his name and image to the game via its box art. It was originally titled Travis Pastrana's Pro MotoX before being renamed MTX: Mototrax featuring Travis Pastrana and eventually settling on its final name.

MTX Mototrax features many of the top AMA Supercross/Motocross racers and X Games freestylers of that time (2004), including Nate Adams, Kenny Bartram, Carey Hart, Chad Reed, Tim Ferry, Mike Brown, Ezra Lusk, among others. The first level in career mode is held at Pastrana's house.

MTX Mototrax supports split-screen multiplayer for up to 2 players and online for up to 8 players. While online support for original Xbox games ended in April 2010, MTX Mototrax is now playable online with Insignia, a revival server restoring online functionality to original Xbox games.
